[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// The `Choice` struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// It is a wrapper around a `u8`, which should have the value either `1` (true)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// or `0` (false).
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// The conversion from `u8` to `Choice` passes the value through an optimization
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// barrier, as a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from inferring that
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// the `Choice` value is a boolean. This strategy is based on Tim Maclean's
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// [work on `rust-timing-shield`][rust-timing-shield], which attempts to provide
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// a more comprehensive approach for preventing software side-channels in Rust
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// code.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)///
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// The `Choice` struct implements operators for AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, to allow
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// combining `Choice` values. These operations do not short-circuit.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// [rust-timing-shield]:
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security
[119](https://docs.rs#119)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
[120](https://docs.rs#120)pub struct Choice(u8);
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)impl Choice {
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// Unwrap the `Choice` wrapper to reveal the underlying `u8`.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    ///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// # Note
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    ///
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// This function only exists as an **escape hatch** for the rare case
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// where it's not possible to use one of the `subtle`-provided
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    /// trait impls.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    ///
[131](https://docs.rs#131)    /// **To convert a `Choice` to a `bool`, use the `From` implementation instead.**
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    #[inline]
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    pub fn unwrap_u8(&self) -> u8 {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        self.0
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)}
[137](https://docs.rs#137)
[138](https://docs.rs#138)impl From<Choice> for bool {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// Convert the `Choice` wrapper into a `bool`, depending on whether
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// the underlying `u8` was a `0` or a `1`.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    ///
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// # Note
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    ///
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    /// This function exists to avoid having higher-level cryptographic protocol
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// implementations duplicating this pattern.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    ///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// The intended use case for this conversion is at the _end_ of a
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// higher-level primitive implementation: for example, in checking a keyed
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// MAC, where the verification should happen in constant-time (and thus use
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// a `Choice`) but it is safe to return a `bool` at the end of the
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// verification.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    #[inline]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    fn from(source: Choice) -> bool {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        debug_assert!((source.0 == 0u8) | (source.0 == 1u8));
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        source.0 != 0
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    }
[157](https://docs.rs#157)}
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)impl BitAnd for Choice {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    type Output = Choice;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    #[inline]
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    fn bitand(self, rhs: Choice) -> Choice {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        (self.0 & rhs.0).into()
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)}
[166](https://docs.rs#166)
[167](https://docs.rs#167)impl BitAndAssign for Choice {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    #[inline]
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    fn bitand_assign(&mut self, rhs: Choice) {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        *self = *self & rhs;
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    }
[172](https://docs.rs#172)}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)
[174](https://docs.rs#174)impl BitOr for Choice {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    type Output = Choice;
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    #[inline]
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    fn bitor(self, rhs: Choice) -> Choice {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        (self.0 | rhs.0).into()
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)}
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)impl BitOrAssign for Choice {
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    #[inline]
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    fn bitor_assign(&mut self, rhs: Choice) {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        *self = *self | rhs;
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)}
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)impl BitXor for Choice {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    type Output = Choice;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    #[inline]
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    fn bitxor(self, rhs: Choice) -> Choice {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        (self.0 ^ rhs.0).into()
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)}
[196](https://docs.rs#196)
[197](https://docs.rs#197)impl BitXorAssign for Choice {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    #[inline]
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    fn bitxor_assign(&mut self, rhs: Choice) {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        *self = *self ^ rhs;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)}
[203](https://docs.rs#203)
[204](https://docs.rs#204)impl Not for Choice {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    type Output = Choice;
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    #[inline]
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    fn not(self) -> Choice {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        (1u8 & (!self.0)).into()
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)}
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// This function is a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from knowing
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// anything about the value of the returned `u8`, other than its type.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)///
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// Because we want to support stable Rust, we don't have access to inline
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// assembly or test::black_box, so we use the fact that volatile values will
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// never be elided to register values.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// Note: Rust's notion of "volatile" is subject to change over time. While this
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// code may break in a non-destructive way in the future, “constant-time” code
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// is a continually moving target, and this is better than doing nothing.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)#[cfg(not(feature = "core_hint_black_box"))]
[223](https://docs.rs#223)#[inline(never)]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)fn black_box<T: Copy>(input: T) -> T {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    unsafe {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        // Optimization barrier
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        //
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        // SAFETY:
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        //   - &input is not NULL because we own input;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        //   - input is Copy and always live;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        //   - input is always properly aligned.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        core::ptr::read_volatile(&input)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)}
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)impl From<u8> for Choice {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    #[inline]
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    fn from(input: u8) -> Choice {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        debug_assert!((input == 0u8) | (input == 1u8));
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        // Our goal is to prevent the compiler from inferring that the value held inside the
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        // resulting `Choice` struct is really a `bool` instead of a `u8`.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        Choice(black_box(input))
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)}
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// An `Eq`-like trait that produces a `Choice` instead of a `bool`.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// # Example
[250](https://docs.rs#250)///
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// ```
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// let x: u8 = 5;
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// let y: u8 = 13;
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&y).unwrap_u8(), 0);
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&x).unwrap_u8(), 1);
[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// ```
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//
[260](https://docs.rs#260)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they
[261](https://docs.rs#261)#[allow(unused_attributes)] // should be in the actual implementation
[262](https://docs.rs#262)pub trait ConstantTimeEq {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// Determine if two items are equal.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// The `ct_eq` function should execute in constant time.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    ///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// # Returns
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// * `Choice(1u8)` if `self == other`;
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// * `Choice(0u8)` if `self != other`.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    #[inline]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    fn ct_eq(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// Determine if two items are NOT equal.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// The `ct_ne` function should execute in constant time.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// # Returns
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// * `Choice(0u8)` if `self == other`;
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// * `Choice(1u8)` if `self != other`.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    #[inline]
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    fn ct_ne(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        !self.ct_eq(other)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)}
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)impl<T: ConstantTimeEq> ConstantTimeEq for [T] {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// Check whether two slices of `ConstantTimeEq` types are equal.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// # Note
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// This function short-circuits if the lengths of the input slices
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// are different.  Otherwise, it should execute in time independent
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// of the slice contents.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// Since arrays coerce to slices, this function works with fixed-size arrays:
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// ```
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// # use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// #
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// let a: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7];
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// let b: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3];
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// let a_eq_a = a.ct_eq(&a);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// let a_eq_b = a.ct_eq(&b);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    ///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// assert_eq!(a_eq_a.unwrap_u8(), 1);
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// assert_eq!(a_eq_b.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// ```
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    #[inline]
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    fn ct_eq(&self, _rhs: &[T]) -> Choice {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        let len = self.len();
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        // Short-circuit on the *lengths* of the slices, not their
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        // contents.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        if len != _rhs.len() {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)            return Choice::from(0);
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        }
[321](https://docs.rs#321)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        // This loop shouldn't be shortcircuitable, since the compiler
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        // shouldn't be able to reason about the value of the `u8`
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        // unwrapped from the `ct_eq` result.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        let mut x = 1u8;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        for (ai, bi) in self.iter().zip(_rhs.iter()) {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)            x &= ai.ct_eq(bi).unwrap_u8();
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        x.into()
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)}
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)impl ConstantTimeEq for Choice {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    #[inline]
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    fn ct_eq(&self, rhs: &Choice) -> Choice {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)        !(*self ^ *rhs)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)}
[340](https://docs.rs#340)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// Given the bit-width `$bit_width` and the corresponding primitive
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// unsigned and signed types `$t_u` and `$t_i` respectively, generate
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// an `ConstantTimeEq` implementation.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)macro_rules! generate_integer_equal {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    ($t_u:ty, $t_i:ty, $bit_width:expr) => {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        impl ConstantTimeEq for $t_u {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)            #[inline]
[348](https://docs.rs#348)            fn ct_eq(&self, other: &$t_u) -> Choice {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                // x == 0 if and only if self == other
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                let x: $t_u = self ^ other;
[351](https://docs.rs#351)
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                // If x == 0, then x and -x are both equal to zero;
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                // otherwise, one or both will have its high bit set.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                let y: $t_u = (x | x.wrapping_neg()) >> ($bit_width - 1);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)                // Result is the opposite of the high bit (now shifted to low).
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                ((y ^ (1 as $t_u)) as u8).into()
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        }
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        impl ConstantTimeEq for $t_i {
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            #[inline]
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            fn ct_eq(&self, other: &$t_i) -> Choice {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                // Bitcast to unsigned and call that implementation.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                (*self as $t_u).ct_eq(&(*other as $t_u))
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    };
[368](https://docs.rs#368)}
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)generate_integer_equal!(u8, i8, 8);
[371](https://docs.rs#371)generate_integer_equal!(u16, i16, 16);
[372](https://docs.rs#372)generate_integer_equal!(u32, i32, 32);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)generate_integer_equal!(u64, i64, 64);
[374](https://docs.rs#374)#[cfg(feature = "i128")]
[375](https://docs.rs#375)generate_integer_equal!(u128, i128, 128);
[376](https://docs.rs#376)generate_integer_equal!(usize, isize, ::core::mem::size_of::<usize>() * 8);

[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// A type which can be conditionally selected in constant time.
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// This trait also provides generic implementations of conditional
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// assignment and conditional swaps.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//
[391](https://docs.rs#391)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they
[392](https://docs.rs#392)#[allow(unused_attributes)] // should be in the actual implementation
[393](https://docs.rs#393)pub trait ConditionallySelectable: Copy {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// Select `a` or `b` according to `choice`.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// # Returns
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// * `a` if `choice == Choice(0)`;
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// * `b` if `choice == Choice(1)`.
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// # Example
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// ```
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// #
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// # fn main() {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// let x: u8 = 13;
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// let y: u8 = 42;
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 0.into());
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// assert_eq!(z, x);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 1.into());
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// assert_eq!(z, y);
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// # }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// ```
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    #[inline]
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self;
[421](https://docs.rs#421)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    /// Conditionally assign `other` to `self`, according to `choice`.
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    ///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// # Example
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// #
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// # fn main() {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// let mut x: u8 = 13;
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// let mut y: u8 = 42;
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    ///
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// x.conditional_assign(&y, 0.into());
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// assert_eq!(x, 13);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// x.conditional_assign(&y, 1.into());
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// assert_eq!(x, 42);
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// # }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// ```
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    #[inline]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    fn conditional_assign(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: Choice) {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        *self = Self::conditional_select(self, other, choice);
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    }
[445](https://docs.rs#445)
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// Conditionally swap `self` and `other` if `choice == 1`; otherwise,
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// reassign both unto themselves.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// # Example
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    ///
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// ```
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    /// #
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// # fn main() {
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// let mut x: u8 = 13;
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// let mut y: u8 = 42;
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    ///
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 0.into());
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// assert_eq!(x, 13);
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    /// assert_eq!(y, 42);
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 1.into());
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// assert_eq!(x, 42);
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// assert_eq!(y, 13);
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    /// # }
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// ```
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    #[inline]
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    fn conditional_swap(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: Choice) {
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        let t: Self = *a;
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        a.conditional_assign(&b, choice);
[472](https://docs.rs#472)        b.conditional_assign(&t, choice);
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    }
[474](https://docs.rs#474)}

[509](https://docs.rs#509)macro_rules! generate_integer_conditional_select {
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    ($($t:tt)*) => ($(
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        impl ConditionallySelectable for $t {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            #[inline]
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self {
[514](https://docs.rs#514)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[515](https://docs.rs#515)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[516](https://docs.rs#516)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[517](https://docs.rs#517)                a ^ (mask & (a ^ b))
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            }
[519](https://docs.rs#519)
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            #[inline]
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            fn conditional_assign(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: Choice) {
[522](https://docs.rs#522)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[523](https://docs.rs#523)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[524](https://docs.rs#524)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[525](https://docs.rs#525)                *self ^= mask & (*self ^ *other);
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            }
[527](https://docs.rs#527)
[528](https://docs.rs#528)            #[inline]
[529](https://docs.rs#529)            fn conditional_swap(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: Choice) {
[530](https://docs.rs#530)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[531](https://docs.rs#531)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[532](https://docs.rs#532)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[533](https://docs.rs#533)                let t = mask & (*a ^ *b);
[534](https://docs.rs#534)                *a ^= t;
[535](https://docs.rs#535)                *b ^= t;
[536](https://docs.rs#536)            }
[537](https://docs.rs#537)         }
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    )*)
[539](https://docs.rs#539)}

[548](https://docs.rs#548)/// `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` where:
[549](https://docs.rs#549)///
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// - `Less` => -1
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// - `Equal` => 0
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// - `Greater` => 1
[553](https://docs.rs#553)///
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// Given this, it's possible to operate on orderings as if they're integers,
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// which allows leveraging conditional masking for predication.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)impl ConditionallySelectable for cmp::Ordering {
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self {
[558](https://docs.rs#558)        let a = *a as i8;
[559](https://docs.rs#559)        let b = *b as i8;
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        let ret = i8::conditional_select(&a, &b, choice);
[561](https://docs.rs#561)
[562](https://docs.rs#562)        // SAFETY: `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` and `ret` has been assigned to
[563](https://docs.rs#563)        // a value which was originally a valid `Ordering` then cast to `i8`
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        unsafe { *((&ret as *const _) as *const cmp::Ordering) }
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    }
[566](https://docs.rs#566)}

[572](https://docs.rs#572)    }

[626](https://docs.rs#626)
[627](https://docs.rs#627)/// The `CtOption<T>` type represents an optional value similar to the
[628](https://docs.rs#628)/// [`Option<T>`](core::option::Option) type but is intended for
[629](https://docs.rs#629)/// use in constant time APIs.
[630](https://docs.rs#630)///
[631](https://docs.rs#631)/// Any given `CtOption<T>` is either `Some` or `None`, but unlike
[632](https://docs.rs#632)/// `Option<T>` these variants are not exposed. The
[633](https://docs.rs#633)/// [`is_some()`](CtOption::is_some) method is used to determine if
[634](https://docs.rs#634)/// the value is `Some`, and [`unwrap_or()`](CtOption::unwrap_or) and
[635](https://docs.rs#635)/// [`unwrap_or_else()`](CtOption::unwrap_or_else) methods are
[636](https://docs.rs#636)/// provided to access the underlying value. The value can also be
[637](https://docs.rs#637)/// obtained with [`unwrap()`](CtOption::unwrap) but this will panic
[638](https://docs.rs#638)/// if it is `None`.
[639](https://docs.rs#639)///
[640](https://docs.rs#640)/// Functions that are intended to be constant time may not produce
[641](https://docs.rs#641)/// valid results for all inputs, such as square root and inversion
[642](https://docs.rs#642)/// operations in finite field arithmetic. Returning an `Option<T>`
[643](https://docs.rs#643)/// from these functions makes it difficult for the caller to reason
[644](https://docs.rs#644)/// about the result in constant time, and returning an incorrect
[645](https://docs.rs#645)/// value burdens the caller and increases the chance of bugs.
[646](https://docs.rs#646)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[647](https://docs.rs#647)pub struct CtOption<T> {
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    value: T,
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    is_some: Choice,
[650](https://docs.rs#650)}
[651](https://docs.rs#651)
[652](https://docs.rs#652)impl<T> From<CtOption<T>> for Option<T> {
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// Convert the `CtOption<T>` wrapper into an `Option<T>`, depending on whether
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    /// the underlying `is_some` `Choice` was a `0` or a `1` once unwrapped.
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    ///
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// # Note
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    ///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// This function exists to avoid ending up with ugly, verbose and/or bad handled
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    /// conversions from the `CtOption<T>` wraps to an `Option<T>` or `Result<T, E>`.
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    /// This implementation doesn't intend to be constant-time nor try to protect the
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// leakage of the `T` since the `Option<T>` will do it anyways.
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    fn from(source: CtOption<T>) -> Option<T> {
[663](https://docs.rs#663)        if source.is_some().unwrap_u8() == 1u8 {
[664](https://docs.rs#664)            Option::Some(source.value)
[665](https://docs.rs#665)        } else {
[666](https://docs.rs#666)            None
[667](https://docs.rs#667)        }
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    }
[669](https://docs.rs#669)}
[670](https://docs.rs#670)
[671](https://docs.rs#671)impl<T> CtOption<T> {
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    /// This method is used to construct a new `CtOption<T>` and takes
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    /// a value of type `T`, and a `Choice` that determines whether
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// the optional value should be `Some` or not. If `is_some` is
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    /// false, the value will still be stored but its value is never
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// exposed.
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    #[inline]

[680](https://docs.rs#680)            value: value,
[681](https://docs.rs#681)            is_some: is_some,
[682](https://docs.rs#682)        }
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    }
[684](https://docs.rs#684)
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// Returns the contained value, consuming the `self` value.
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    ///
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    /// # Panics
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    ///
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// Panics if the value is none with a custom panic message provided by
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// `msg`.
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    pub fn expect(self, msg: &str) -> T {
[692](https://docs.rs#692)        assert_eq!(self.is_some.unwrap_u8(), 1, "{}", msg);
[693](https://docs.rs#693)
[694](https://docs.rs#694)        self.value
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    }
[696](https://docs.rs#696)

[699](https://docs.rs#699)    #[inline]
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    pub fn unwrap(self) -> T {

[704](https://docs.rs#704)    }
[705](https://docs.rs#705)
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// This returns the underlying value if it is `Some`

[708](https://docs.rs#708)    #[inline]
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    pub fn unwrap_or(self, def: T) -> T
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    where
[711](https://docs.rs#711)        T: ConditionallySelectable,
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    {
[713](https://docs.rs#713)        T::conditional_select(&def, &self.value, self.is_some)
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    }
[715](https://docs.rs#715)

[718](https://docs.rs#718)    ///

[721](https://docs.rs#721)    #[inline]
[722](https://docs.rs#722)    pub fn unwrap_or_else<F>(self, f: F) -> T

[730](https://docs.rs#730)    /// Returns a true `Choice` if this value is `Some`.
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    #[inline]
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    pub fn is_some(&self) -> Choice {
[733](https://docs.rs#733)        self.is_some
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    }
[735](https://docs.rs#735)
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    /// Returns a true `Choice` if this value is `None`.
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    #[inline]
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    pub fn is_none(&self) -> Choice {

[740](https://docs.rs#740)    }
[741](https://docs.rs#741)
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// Returns a `None` value if the option is `None`, otherwise
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// returns a `CtOption` enclosing the value of the provided closure.
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// The closure is given the enclosed value or, if the option is
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    /// `None`, it is provided a dummy value computed using
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// `Default::default()`.
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///

[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be greater

[843](https://docs.rs#843)pub trait ConstantTimeGreater {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)    /// Determine whether `self > other`.
[845](https://docs.rs#845)    ///
[846](https://docs.rs#846)    /// The bitwise-NOT of the return value of this function should be usable to
[847](https://docs.rs#847)    /// determine if `self <= other`.
[848](https://docs.rs#848)    ///
[849](https://docs.rs#849)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[850](https://docs.rs#850)    ///
[851](https://docs.rs#851)    /// # Returns
[852](https://docs.rs#852)    ///
[853](https://docs.rs#853)    /// A `Choice` with a set bit if `self > other`, and with no set bits
[854](https://docs.rs#854)    /// otherwise.
[855](https://docs.rs#855)    ///
[856](https://docs.rs#856)    /// # Example
[857](https://docs.rs#857)    ///
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    /// ```
[859](https://docs.rs#859)    /// use subtle::ConstantTimeGreater;
[860](https://docs.rs#860)    ///
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    /// let x: u8 = 13;
[862](https://docs.rs#862)    /// let y: u8 = 42;
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    ///
[864](https://docs.rs#864)    /// let x_gt_y = x.ct_gt(&y);
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    ///
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    /// assert_eq!(x_gt_y.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    ///
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    /// let y_gt_x = y.ct_gt(&x);
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    ///
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    /// assert_eq!(y_gt_x.unwrap_u8(), 1);
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    ///
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    /// let x_gt_x = x.ct_gt(&x);
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    ///
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    /// assert_eq!(x_gt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    /// ```
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    fn ct_gt(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice;
[877](https://docs.rs#877)}
[878](https://docs.rs#878)
[879](https://docs.rs#879)macro_rules! generate_unsigned_integer_greater {
[880](https://docs.rs#880)    ($t_u: ty, $bit_width: expr) => {
[881](https://docs.rs#881)        impl ConstantTimeGreater for $t_u {
[882](https://docs.rs#882)            /// Returns Choice::from(1) iff x > y, and Choice::from(0) iff x <= y.
[883](https://docs.rs#883)            ///
[884](https://docs.rs#884)            /// # Note
[885](https://docs.rs#885)            ///
[886](https://docs.rs#886)            /// This algoritm would also work for signed integers if we first
[887](https://docs.rs#887)            /// flip the top bit, e.g. `let x: u8 = x ^ 0x80`, etc.
[888](https://docs.rs#888)            #[inline]
[889](https://docs.rs#889)            fn ct_gt(&self, other: &$t_u) -> Choice {
[890](https://docs.rs#890)                let gtb = self & !other; // All the bits in self that are greater than their corresponding bits in other.
[891](https://docs.rs#891)                let mut ltb = !self & other; // All the bits in self that are less than their corresponding bits in other.
[892](https://docs.rs#892)                let mut pow = 1;
[893](https://docs.rs#893)
[894](https://docs.rs#894)                // Less-than operator is okay here because it's dependent on the bit-width.
[895](https://docs.rs#895)                while pow < $bit_width {
[896](https://docs.rs#896)                    ltb |= ltb >> pow; // Bit-smear the highest set bit to the right.
[897](https://docs.rs#897)                    pow += pow;
[898](https://docs.rs#898)                }
[899](https://docs.rs#899)                let mut bit = gtb & !ltb; // Select the highest set bit.
[900](https://docs.rs#900)                let mut pow = 1;
[901](https://docs.rs#901)
[902](https://docs.rs#902)                while pow < $bit_width {
[903](https://docs.rs#903)                    bit |= bit >> pow; // Shift it to the right until we end up with either 0 or 1.
[904](https://docs.rs#904)                    pow += pow;
[905](https://docs.rs#905)                }
[906](https://docs.rs#906)                // XXX We should possibly do the above flattening to 0 or 1 in the
[907](https://docs.rs#907)                //     Choice constructor rather than making it a debug error?
[908](https://docs.rs#908)                Choice::from((bit & 1) as u8)
[909](https://docs.rs#909)            }
[910](https://docs.rs#910)        }
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    };
[912](https://docs.rs#912)}

# Choice in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/latest/target-redirect/subtle/struct.Choice.html

`pub struct Choice(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

The `Choice` struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.

It is a wrapper around a `u8`, which should have the value either `1` (true)
or `0` (false).

The conversion from `u8` to `Choice` passes the value through an optimization
barrier, as a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from inferring that
the `Choice` value is a boolean. This strategy is based on Tim Maclean’s
[work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security), which attempts to provide
a more comprehensive approach for preventing software side-channels in Rust
code.

The `Choice` struct implements operators for AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, to allow
combining `Choice` values. These operations do not short-circuit.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#568-573)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Choice)### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#568-573)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Choice)

### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#119)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-Choice)

Convert the `Choice` wrapper into a `bool`, depending on whether
the underlying `u8` was a `0` or a `1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-1)Note

This function exists to avoid having higher-level cryptographic protocol implementations duplicating this pattern.

The intended use case for this conversion is at the *end* of a
higher-level primitive implementation: for example, in checking a keyed
MAC, where the verification should happen in constant-time (and thus use
a `Choice`) but it is safe to return a `bool` at the end of the
verification.

# CtOption in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/latest/target-redirect/subtle/struct.CtOption.html

`pub struct CtOption<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `CtOption<T>` type represents an optional value similar to the
[ Option<T>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html) type but is intended for
use in constant time APIs.

Any given `CtOption<T>` is either `Some` or `None`, but unlike
`Option<T>` these variants are not exposed. The
[ is_some()](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.is_some) method is used to determine if
the value is

`Some`, and [and](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap_or)

`unwrap_or()`[methods are provided to access the underlying value. The value can also be obtained with](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap_or_else)

`unwrap_or_else()`[but this will panic if it is](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap)

`unwrap()``None`.Functions that are intended to be constant time may not produce
valid results for all inputs, such as square root and inversion
operations in finite field arithmetic. Returning an `Option<T>`
from these functions makes it difficult for the caller to reason
about the result in constant time, and returning an incorrect
value burdens the caller and increases the chance of bugs.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

This method is used to construct a new `CtOption<T>` and takes
a value of type `T`, and a `Choice` that determines whether
the optional value should be `Some` or not. If `is_some` is
false, the value will still be stored but its value is never
exposed.

This returns the underlying value if it is `Some`
or the provided value otherwise.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#722-728)#### pub fn [unwrap_or_else](https://docs.rs#method.unwrap_or_else)<F>(self, f: F) -> T

#### pub fn [into_option](https://docs.rs#method.into_option)(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

Convert the `CtOption<T>` wrapper into an `Option<T>`, depending on whether
the underlying `is_some` `Choice` was a `0` or a `1` once unwrapped.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This function exists to avoid ending up with ugly, verbose and/or bad handled
conversions from the `CtOption<T>` wraps to an `Option<T>` or `Result<T, E>`.
This implementation doesn’t intend to be constant-time nor try to protect the
leakage of the `T` since the `Option<T>` will do it anyways.

It’s equivalent to the corresponding `From` impl, however this version is
friendlier for type inference.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#420)#### fn [conditional_select](https://docs.rs#tymethod.conditional_select)(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#420)

#### fn [conditional_select](https://docs.rs#tymethod.conditional_select)(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) -> Self

Select `a` or `b` according to `choice`.

[§](https://docs.rs#returns)Returns

- `a`if- `choice == Choice(0)`;
- `b`if- `choice == Choice(1)`.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let x: u8 = 13;
let y: u8 = 42;
let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(z, x);
let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(z, y);
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#442-444)#### fn [conditional_assign](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_assign)(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

#### fn [conditional_assign](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_assign)(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

Conditionally assign `other` to `self`, according to `choice`.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let mut x: u8 = 13;
let mut y: u8 = 42;
x.conditional_assign(&y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(x, 13);
x.conditional_assign(&y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(x, 42);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#469-473)#### fn [conditional_swap](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_swap)(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#469-473)

#### fn [conditional_swap](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_swap)(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

Conditionally swap `self` and `other` if `choice == 1`; otherwise,
reassign both unto themselves.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let mut x: u8 = 13;
let mut y: u8 = 42;
u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(x, 13);
assert_eq!(y, 42);
u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(x, 42);
assert_eq!(y, 13);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConstantTimeEq-for-%5BT%5D)

### impl<T: [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html)> [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) for [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)

Check whether two slices of `ConstantTimeEq` types are equal.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This function short-circuits if the lengths of the input slices are different. Otherwise, it should execute in time independent of the slice contents.

Since arrays coerce to slices, this function works with fixed-size arrays:

```
let a: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7];
let b: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3];
let a_eq_a = a.ct_eq(&a);
let a_eq_b = a.ct_eq(&b);
assert_eq!(a_eq_a.unwrap_u8(), 1);
assert_eq!(a_eq_b.unwrap_u8(), 0);
```

# ConstantTimeLess in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/latest/target-redirect/subtle/trait.ConstantTimeLess.html

`pub trait ConstantTimeLess: `[ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) + [ConstantTimeGreater](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeGreater.html) {
    // Provided method
    fn [ct_lt](https://docs.rs#method.ct_lt)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be less than another of the same type.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Determine whether `self < other`.

The bitwise-NOT of the return value of this function should be usable to
determine if `self >= other`.

A default implementation is provided and implemented for the unsigned integer types.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#returns)Returns

A `Choice` with a set bit if `self < other`, and with no set bits
otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConstantTimeLess;
let x: u8 = 13;
let y: u8 = 42;
let x_lt_y = x.ct_lt(&y);
assert_eq!(x_lt_y.unwrap_u8(), 1);
let y_lt_x = y.ct_lt(&x);
assert_eq!(y_lt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
let x_lt_x = x.ct_lt(&x);
assert_eq!(x_lt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2

## Expand description

`clap` is a simple-to-use, efficient, and full-featured library for parsing command line
arguments and subcommands when writing console/terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user
at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means
you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of
arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) ‘for free’ meaning
automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking the list of valid possibilities you
supplied and adding only the ones you haven’t already defined. If you are using subcommands,
`clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any
applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and
exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to
exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of
the arguments.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`.
For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and
occurrences see the [documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/), [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of
this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl2Z5T8g1pRkIynR3E0_pc7U).

**NOTE:** All of these examples are functionally the same, but show different styles in which to
use `clap`

The first example shows a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it’s more verbose.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is
// more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility
// to generate arguments dynamically.
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("My Super Program")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("config")
                               .short("c")
                               .long("config")
                               .value_name("FILE")
                               .help("Sets a custom config file")
                               .takes_value(true))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT")
                               .help("Sets the input file to use")
                               .required(true)
                               .index(1))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("v")
                               .short("v")
                               .multiple(true)
                               .help("Sets the level of verbosity"))
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg(Arg::with_name("debug")
                                          .short("d")
                                          .help("print debug information verbosely")))
                          .get_matches();
    // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf"
    let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf");
    println!("Value for config: {}", config);
    // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't
    // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value)
    println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap());
    // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag
    // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v'
    match matches.occurrences_of("v") {
        0 => println!("No verbose info"),
        1 => println!("Some verbose info"),
        2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"),
        3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"),
    }
    // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name
    // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time
    if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") {
        if matches.is_present("debug") {
            println!("Printing debug info...");
        } else {
            println!("Printing normally...");
        }
    }
    // more program logic goes here...
}
```
The next example shows a far less verbose method, but sacrifices some of the advanced
configuration options (not shown in this small example). This method also takes a *very* minor
runtime penalty.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments
// which is less verbose
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("myapp")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .args_from_usage(
                              "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file'
                              <INPUT>              'Sets the input file to use'
                              -v...                'Sets the level of verbosity'")
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'"))
                          .get_matches();
    // Same as previous example...
}
```
This third method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization.

First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we
like:

```
name: myapp
version: "1.0"
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: "1.3"
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Since this feature requires additional dependencies that not everyone may want, it is *not*
compiled in by default and we need to enable a feature flag in Cargo.toml:

Simply change your `clap = "~2.27.0"` to `clap = {version = "~2.27.0", features = ["yaml"]}`.

At last we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far
// more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods.
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
    // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found
    let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml");
    let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches();
    // Same as previous examples...
}
```
Finally there is a macro version, which is like a hybrid approach offering the speed of the builder pattern (the first example), but without all the verbosity.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
fn main() {
    let matches = clap_app!(myapp =>
        (version: "1.0")
        (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
        (about: "Does awesome things")
        (@arg CONFIG: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file")
        (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use")
        (@arg debug: -d ... "Sets the level of debugging information")
        (@subcommand test =>
            (about: "controls testing features")
            (version: "1.3")
            (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
            (@arg verbose: -v --verbose "Print test information verbosely")
        )
    ).get_matches();
    // Same as before...
}
```
If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or
`help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

```
$ myprog --help
My Super Program 1.0
Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
Does awesome things
USAGE:
    MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND]
FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints this message
    -v               Sets the level of verbosity
    -V, --version    Prints version information
OPTIONS:
    -c, --config <FILE>    Sets a custom config file
ARGS:
    INPUT    The input file to use
SUBCOMMANDS:
    help    Prints this message
    test    Controls testing features
```
**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the
`test` subcommand.

- `suggestions`: Turns on the- `Did you mean '--myoption'?`feature for when users make typos. (builds dependency- `strsim`)
- `color`: Turns on colored error messages. This feature only works on non-Windows OSs. (builds dependency- `ansi-term`and- `atty`)
- `wrap_help`: Wraps the help at the actual terminal width when available, instead of 120 characters. (builds dependency- `textwrap`with feature- `term_size`)

To disable these, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
```
You can also selectively enable only the features you’d like to include, by adding:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
# Cherry-pick the features you'd like to use
features = [ "suggestions", "color" ]
```
- **“yaml”**: Enables building CLIs from YAML documents. (builds dependency- `yaml-rust`)
- **“unstable”**: Enables unstable- `clap`features that may change from release to release

There are a few goals of `clap` that I’d like to maintain throughout contributions. If your
proposed changes break, or go against any of these goals we’ll discuss the changes further
before merging (but will *not* be ignored, all contributes are welcome!). These are by no means
hard-and-fast rules, as I’m no expert and break them myself from time to time (even if by
mistake or ignorance).

- Remain backwards compatible when possible
- If backwards compatibility *must*be broken, use deprecation warnings if at all possible before removing legacy code - This does not apply for security concerns

- If backwards compatibility
- Parse arguments quickly
- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although *slightly*less stringent, as the program is about to exit)

- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although
- Try to be cognizant of memory usage
- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of `clap`should be low since the main program is the star of the show

- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of
- `panic!`on- *developer*error, exit gracefully on- *end-user*error

Because `clap` takes `SemVer` and compatibility seriously, this is the official policy regarding
breaking changes and previous versions of Rust.

`clap` will pin the minimum required version of Rust to the CI builds. Bumping the minimum
version of Rust is considered a minor breaking change, meaning *at a minimum* the minor version
of `clap` will be bumped.

In order to keep from being surprised by breaking changes, it is **highly** recommended to use
the `~major.minor.patch` style in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies] clap = "~2.27.0"
```
This will cause *only* the patch version to be updated upon a `cargo update` call, and therefore
cannot break due to new features, or bumped minimum versions of Rust.

`clap` will officially support current stable Rust, minus two releases, but may work with prior
releases as well. For example, current stable Rust at the time of this writing is 1.21.0,
meaning `clap` is guaranteed to compile with 1.19.0 and beyond. At the 1.22.0 release, `clap`
will be guaranteed to compile with 1.20.0 and beyond, etc.

Upon bumping the minimum version of Rust (assuming it’s within the stable-2 range), it *must* be
clearly annotated in the `CHANGELOG.md`

`clap` is licensed under the MIT license. Please read the [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v2.34.0/LICENSE-MIT) file in
this repository for more information.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3

A simple to use, efficient, and full featured library for parsing command line arguments and subcommands when writing console, or terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) 'for free' meaning automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking list of valid possibilities you supplied and adding only the ones you haven't already defined. If you are using subcommands, `clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of the arguments.

For a full FAQ and more in depth details, see [the wiki page](https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs/wiki/FAQ)

First, let me say that these comparisons are highly subjective, and not meant in a critical or harsh manner. All the argument parsing libraries out there (to include `clap`) have their own strengths and weaknesses. Sometimes it just comes down to personal taste when all other factors are equal. When in doubt, try them all and pick one that you enjoy :) There's plenty of room in the Rust community for multiple implementations!

`getopts` is a very basic, fairly minimalist argument parsing library. This isn't a bad thing, sometimes you don't need tons of features, you just want to parse some simple arguments, and have some help text generated for you based on valid arguments you specify. The downside to this approach is that you must manually implement most of the common features (such as checking to display help messages, usage strings, etc.). If you want a highly custom argument parser, and don't mind writing the majority of the functionality yourself, `getopts` is an excellent base.

`getopts` also doesn't allocate much, or at all. This gives it a very small performance boost. Although, as you start implementing additional features, that boost quickly disappears.

Personally, I find many, many uses of `getopts` are manually implementing features that `clap` provides by default. Using `clap` simplifies your codebase allowing you to focus on your application, and not argument parsing.

I first want to say I'm a big a fan of BurntSushi's work, the creator of `Docopt.rs`. I aspire to produce the quality of libraries that this man does! When it comes to comparing these two libraries they are very different. `docopt` tasks you with writing a help message, and then it parsers that message for you to determine all valid arguments and their use. Some people LOVE this approach, others do not. If you're willing to write a detailed help message, it's nice that you can stick that in your program and have `docopt` do the rest. On the downside, it's far less flexible.

`docopt` is also excellent at translating arguments into Rust types automatically. There is even a syntax extension which will do all this for you, if you're willing to use a nightly compiler (use of a stable compiler requires you to somewhat manually translate from arguments to Rust types). To use BurntSushi's words, `docopt` is also a sort of black box. You get what you get, and it's hard to tweak implementation or customize the experience for your use case.

Because `docopt` is doing a ton of work to parse your help messages and determine what you were trying to communicate as valid arguments, it's also one of the more heavy weight parsers performance-wise. For most applications this isn't a concern and this isn't to say `docopt` is slow, in fact from it. This is just something to keep in mind while comparing.

`clap` is as fast, and as lightweight as possible while still giving all the features you'd expect from a modern argument parser. In fact, for the amount and type of features `clap` offers it remains about as fast as `getopts`. If you use `clap` when just need some simple arguments parsed, you'll find its a walk in the park. `clap` also makes it possible to represent extremely complex, and advanced requirements, without too much thought. `clap` aims to be intuitive, easy to use, and fully capable for wide variety use cases and needs.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`. For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and occurrences see the [documentation](http://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/clap/index.html), [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl0Bc_EU_pBNcX-rhVqDTRxv) (which are quite outdated by now).

**NOTE:** All these examples are functionally the same, but show three different styles in which to use `clap`

The following example is show a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it's more verbose.

use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand}; fn main() { let matches = App::new("My Super Program") .version("1.0") .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") .about("Does awesome things") .arg(Arg::with_name("config") .short("c") .long("config") .value_name("FILE") .help("Sets a custom config file") .takes_value(true)) .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT") .help("Sets the input file to use") .required(true) .index(1)) .arg(Arg::with_name("v") .short("v") .multiple(true) .help("Sets the level of verbosity")) .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test") .about("controls testing features") .version("1.3") .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") .arg(Arg::with_name("debug") .short("d") .help("print debug information verbosely"))) .get_matches(); // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v' match matches.occurrences_of("v") { 0 => println!("No verbose info"), 1 => println!("Some verbose info"), 2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"), 3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"), } // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") { if matches.is_present("debug") { println!("Printing debug info..."); } else { println!("Printing normally..."); } } // more program logic goes here... }

The following example is functionally the same as the one above, but shows a far less verbose method but sacrifices some of the advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example).

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments which is less // less verbose extern crate clap; use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand}; fn main() { let matches = App::new("myapp") .version("1.0") .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") .about("Does awesome things") .args_from_usage( "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file' <INPUT> 'Sets the input file to use' -v... 'Sets the level of verbosity'") .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test") .about("controls testing features") .version("1.3") .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'")) .get_matches(); // Same as previous example... }

The following combines the previous two examples by using the less verbose `from_usage` methods and the performance of the Builder Pattern.

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01c_quick_example.rs) // Must be compiled with `--features unstable` // // This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments which is less // less verbose #[macro_use] extern crate clap; fn main() { let matches = clap_app!(myapp => (version: "1.0") (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") (about: "Does awesome things") (@arg config: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file") (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use") (@arg verbose: -v ... "Sets the level of verbosity") (@subcommand test => (about: "controls testing features") (version: "1.3") (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") (@arg verbose: -d --debug "Print debug information") ) ).get_matches(); // Same as previous examples... }

This final method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization. First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we like (we'll use the same both examples above to keep it functionally equivalent):

```
name: myapp
version: 1.0
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: 1.3
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Now we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far // more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods. #[macro_use] extern crate clap; use clap::App; fn main() { // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml"); let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches(); // Same as previous examples... }

**NOTE**: The YAML and macro builder options require adding a special `features` flag when compiling `clap` because they are not compiled by default. Simply change your `clap = "2"` to `clap = {version = "2", features = ["yaml"]}` for YAML, or `features = ["unstable"]` for the macro builder, in your `Cargo.toml`.

If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or `help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

$ myprog --help My Super Program 1.0 Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com> Does awesome things USAGE: MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND] FLAGS: -h, --help Prints this message -v Sets the level of verbosity -V, --version Prints version information OPTIONS: -c, --config <FILE> Sets a custom config file ARGS: INPUT The input file to use SUBCOMMANDS: help Prints this message test Controls testing features

**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the `test` subcommand.

To try out the pre-built example, use the following steps:

- Clone the repository `$ git clone https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs && cd clap-rs/clap-tests`
- Compile the example `$ cargo build --release`
- Run the help info `$ ./target/release/claptests --help`
- Play with the arguments!

To test out `clap`'s default auto-generated help/version follow these steps:
* Create a new cargo project `$ cargo new fake --bin && cd fake`
* Add `clap` to your `Cargo.toml`
*
`toml [dependencies] clap = "2"`

- Add the following to your `src/main.rs`

extern crate clap; use clap::App; fn main() { App::new("fake").version("v1.0-beta").get_matches(); }

- Build your program `$ cargo build --release`
- Run with help or version `$ ./target/release/fake --help`or`$ ./target/release/fake --version`

For full usage, add `clap` as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml` file to use from crates.io:

```
 [dependencies]
 clap = "2"
```
Or track the latest on the master branch at github:

```
[dependencies.clap]
git = "https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs.git"
```
Add `extern crate clap;` to your crate root.

Define a list of valid arguments for your program (see the [documentation](https://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/index.html) or [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repo)

Then run `cargo build` or `cargo update && cargo build` for your project.

If you'd like to keep your dependency list to **only** `clap`, you can disable any features that require an additional dependency. To do this, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "2"
default-features = false
```
You can also selectively enable only the features you'd like to include, by adding:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "2"
default-features = false
# Cherry-pick the features you'd like to use
features = [ "suggestions", "color" ]
```
The following is a list of optional `clap` features:

- **"suggestions"**: Turns on the- `Did you mean '--myoption'?`feature for when users make typos.
- **"color"**: Turns on colored error messages. This feature only works on non-Windows OSs.
- **"lints"**: This is- **not**included by default and should only be used while developing to run basic lints against changes. This can only be used on Rust nightly.
- **"debug"**: This is- **not**included by default and should only be used while developing to display debugging information.
- **"yaml"**: This is- **not**included by default. Enables building CLIs from YAML documents.
- **"unstable"**: This is- **not**included by default. Enables unstable features, unstable refers to whether or not they may change, not performance stability.

You can find complete documentation on the [github-pages site](http://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/clap/index.html) for this project.

You can also find usage examples in the [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repo.

There's also the video tutorial series [Argument Parsing with Rust](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl0Bc_EU_pBNcX-rhVqDTRxv) that I've been working on.

*Note*: Two new videos have just been added ([08 From Usage](https://youtu.be/xc6VdedFrG0), and [09 Typed Values](https://youtu.be/mZn3C1DnD90)), if you're already familiar with `clap` but want to know more about these two details you can check out those videos without watching the previous few.

*Note*: Apologies for the resolution of the first video, it will be updated to a better resolution soon. The other videos have a proper resolution.

If contributing, you can run the tests as follows (assuming you're in the `clap-rs` directory)

$ cargo test && make -C clap-tests test $ cargo test --features yaml $ cargo build --features lints
